scenes.title: Make a plan, then review it
An offer is not yet an agreement

captions.text: How do you prepare for a job you have never done?
LearnSprint lets you practice a fictional first shift in operations, where your decisions change the plan.
Three orders share limited stock and delivery departures.
I ask the warehouse what is available.
The reply points to scenario facts, so I can distinguish confirmed stock from an expected arrival.
I allocate the kits and review the whole board.
The application checks inventory over time, carrier capacity, order quantities, deadlines, and shipping cost.
I decide when to record this plan.
Then the supplier is delayed.
The earlier review stays in the record, but it no longer describes the current facts.
I need to respond to the changed situation.
Customer B can accept a split delivery.
Asking reveals the offer; I must explicitly record the agreement before it changes the constraints.
I move twenty kits to tomorrow and review the recovery plan.
The handoff preserves my plan, its assumptions, and unresolved issues.
This is evidence of decisions inside a simulation, not a claim that parcels were delivered or that I am ready for a job.
A linked replay changes the opening stock and customer terms.
It starts with a clean board and keeps its own help history.
The report compares the saved decisions, rather than treating a repeated answer as proof of learning.
Amazon Bedrock Nova Two Lite interprets a typed request into one bounded allocation proposal.
I see the exact edit, choose Apply, and can Undo.
The application still owns the facts and checks.
This Alexa Plus style web simulation runs on AWS.
Browser voice remains a prototype.
Next comes practitioner review and a learner pilot.
LearnSprint: practice the work before the first job.
